                    ### Question
                    A 42-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 10-month history of joint pain and stiffness in her wrists and fingers. The symptoms are worse in the morning and improve with activity. Physical examination shows swelling and warmth over the MCP and wrist joints in both hands. An x-ray of the hands is shown. Synovial biopsy from an affected joint would most likely show which of the following?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Noninflammatory superficial fibrin deposits
opb. Monosodium urate crystals
opc. Calcium pyrophosphate crystals
opd. Noncaseating granulomas
ope. Proliferation of granulation tissue

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of a 42-year-old woman with joint pain and stiffness, particularly worse in the morning and improving with activity, is highly suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). The physical examination findings of swelling and warmth over the MCP and wrist joints further support this diagnosis. In RA, a synovial biopsy typically reveals inflammatory changes characterized by the proliferation of granulation tissue, which is consistent with the autoimmune nature of the disease. The retrieved evidence paths confirm that inflammation is associated with granulation tissue formation in the context of RA. Therefore, the most likely finding in the synovial biopsy would be the proliferation of granulation tissue.
